title: Andersen et al., The Impact of Tutorials on Games of Varying Complexity (CHI 2012)
label: research
claim: Eight tutorial designs in three games, 45,000+ players. Tutorials raised play time up to 29% (progress up to 75%) in the most complex game (Foldit); no significant engagement gain in the two simpler games. Authors: tutorial investment may not be justified where mechanics can be discovered by experiment. Project page does not list the eight designs.

title: Different types of Tutorials (Game Developer)
label: practitioner
claim: Distinguishes instructions, examples, and a carefully designed experience (SMB 1-1). Tutorial value depends on game complexity; active-learning tutorials fail when the player has no isolated place to practise a complex skill; Braid shows its rewind help after the first death, i.e. when first necessary; no single best method. Does not address skipping.

title: Design Philosophy: Shigeru Miyamoto (blakecrosley.com)
label: opinion
claim: Secondary commentary: 1-1 first Goomba approaches at walking pace, first mushroom is boxed so it slides into the player, pits appear only after the tools to cross them. No primary Miyamoto quote; attribution of intent unverified.

title: Baba Is You Steam discussions (Lake levels order)
label: verbatim
claim: Players say a level that looks like a tutorial is placed after players already had to work the thing out; another thread complains a level needed an interaction not yet shown. Teach-after-need is perceived as order error. Only snippets seen.

title: Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019, Matthew Davis)
label: snippet
claim: Billed topics: cutting features, difficulty, randomness; tutorial design not listed. Justin Ma (RPS, via repost) said the team gave up appealing ideas to keep the game clear: a feature is in if it can be shown clearly. Talk is members-only; not read.

title: Expertise reversal effect / worked-example search results
label: research
claim: Guidance that helps novices becomes redundant and harmful for those with more knowledge (Kalyuga); unguided search loads novices' working memory; remedy in the literature is fading supports adaptively. One legal-reasoning study found no reversal for less-structured tasks. No game-specific study seen.

title: Portal developer commentary transcript (fan wiki hosting Valve's in-game commentary)
label: developer
claim: Walker: Portal is 'effectively an extended player training exercise'. Swift: playtesters assumed portals led to other dimensions, so the start room is made memorable. Davis: testers assumed orange portals were exit-only, so a puzzle was added. Chin: playtesting showed a puzzle 'introduced too many new concepts at once'. Barnett: 'without some serious prompting, players will rarely look up.' Transcript hosted by a wiki, speech is Valve's.

title: Thinking with Portals: Making a Test Chamber (Game Informer, 2010)
label: developer
claim: Valve trains in two stages: 'checklisting' breaks a new mechanic into the core components players must grasp, in 'a very clean room to safely experiment with it'; then challenges 'take a previously learned rule and turn it on its head'. Playtesting is how they verify the teaching worked; when testers miss a required element the element is made more noticeable.

title: Wayline: eternal beta, bad retention loops
label: practitioner
claim: Unnamed game: tutorial completion 55% to 85% and early churn down 20% after splitting the tutorial into chunks with a goal and immediate reward each and adding action-sensitive tooltips. No sample size, no control group; not attributable.

label: developer

claim: Null: no Team Cherry statement found. Players debate whether pogo is taught; one reply says the spike room is built so you know to use spikes. Learning-by-level-design is asserted by critics only.

title: Andersen et al., Impact of Tutorials on Games of Varying Complexity (CHI 2012), full PDF
label: research
claim: 45,000+ players, 8 conditions, Refraction, Hello Worlds, Foldit. Foldit: tutorials raised play time up to 29%, progress up to 75%; negligible effect in the other two. Context-sensitive instructions: +16% play time, +40% progress in Foldit, no effect elsewhere. No evidence that restricting freedom helps. On-demand help helped Foldit, no effect in Hello Worlds, NEGATIVE in Refraction. Conclusion: players of experimentable games seem to learn more from experimentation than from reading text.

title: Iwata Asks: New Super Mario Bros. Wii, Vol 1 part 4 (Nakago, Tezuka, Iwata), full page
label: developer
claim: Nakago: levels were not made from screen one; World 3 or 5 came first, and beginners found them incredibly difficult, so 'our basic principle is to move easier features to the beginning of the level'. 1-1 was designed so the player always gets the mushroom (first pipe placed because the mushroom bounces off it); planned on paper with fallback paths; created at the end and adjusted until the last minute. Iwata: at release players did not read the manual, so the game was built for beginners to learn naturally. The page does not say Miyamoto described the forced mushroom as showing it differs from a Goomba.

title: Kalyuga 2007, Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction (Educ Psychol Rev), full PDF
label: research
claim: Designs effective for low-knowledge learners can lose effect or have negative consequences for proficient ones. Conclusion: replicated across many materials and participants (2,200+ students; effect sizes 0.45 to 2.99), full reversal or more often partial; reversal usually shown cross-sectionally; guidance should be given at the appropriate time and unnecessary support removed as learners progress; adaptive tailoring has best potential. Limits: few studies of optimal methods, mostly well-defined technical domains.
